Institutions are rules in equilibrium: correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria, which the players represent to themselves as rules. | [LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle (2006), DOI-10.1177/1463499606061731. Institutional reality is built from three primitives: collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in C". The Y status is held only by collective acceptance, and it carries deontic powers, which are desire-independent reasons for action. Institutional facts need language because they exist only as represented. Two revisions of the 1995 book: status indicators (after De Soto), and "free-standing Y terms" (after Barry Smith), such as corporations and money without currency. In those cases there is no X, and "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is ranked as the more general form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md)), in its parallel English printing in Papers: Revista de Sociologia 80 (2006), pp. 51–71, not in the Anthropological Theory typesetting the DOI names; worth reading as Searle's own short restatement of The Construction of Social Reality ([LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md)), and as the place where he concedes that "X counts as Y in C" is not the general form. | [LIT-486](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-486.md) | Social Structures and the Ontology of Social Groups | Ritchie (2018 online; PPR 100(2), 2020). Social structures are networks of relations constitutively, not merely causally, dependent on social factors, and can be overt or covert, intentionally or unintentionally created, internal or external to what realizes them. Organized social groups (teams, courts, families) are structured wholes with internal social structures whose nodes people occupy; feature social groups (women, racial groups, classes) are social kinds, nodes in external social structures. Both meet a "Goldilocks Constraint": intuitive and explanatory groups in, arbitrary collections out. | [LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md) | Social Ontology | Epstein (2018; rev. 2024), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/social-ontology/>. A survey that splits social ontology into two inquiries: what determines (grounds) a social fact, and what constructs or "anchors" the category it falls under, likened to semantics and metasemantics. §3 surveys determination bases (psychologism, atomism, bodies and practices, physicalism, holism, flat ontologies) and reports that ontological individualism is widely assumed and recently contested. §4 surveys anchoring theories (agreement, Lewis's convention, Hart and Searle's collective acceptance, patterns, practices, language). §5 covers groups, group minds and agency, institutions, race and gender, artifacts, money, law and language. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-393](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-393.md)); worth reading as a survey: the best single map of social ontology in the record, organised around its author's distinction between what grounds a social fact (§3) and what anchors, or sets up, the category it falls under (§4). It is also the record's readable source for what The Ant Trap's grounding–anchoring framework is ([LIT-478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-478.md) is not lawfully readable). Read it as a survey written by a partisan: Epstein's own positions organise the entry, and the critics of anchoring are named but given a sentence each. |
| [LIT-488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-488.md) v2 | Shared Agency: A Planning Theory of Acting Together | Bratman (2014), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199897933.001.0001. The planning structures that organise an individual's agency over time are also at the core of small-scale shared agency. A shared intention is constructed from each participant's intention that "we J", by way of each other's intentions and meshing subplans, with persistence interdependence and common knowledge. These conditions are offered as sufficient, not necessary. No group subject and no new primitive is needed: the account is reductive "in spirit", against Gilbert and Searle. Unread: filed from the chapter list and the author's précis. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata, the chapter list and the author's open-access précis; no lawful full text of the book was reachable (Oxford Academic is paywalled, and Bratman has not posted the book or draft chapters), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the developed statement of the reductive, planning-theory account of shared agency, and the précis, read in full, says plainly where it parts from Gilbert and Searle. |
| [LIT-489](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-489.md) | Institutions | North (1991), DOI-10.1257/jep.5.1.97. Institutions are "the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction": informal constraints (taboos, customs, codes of conduct) and formal rules (constitutions, laws, property rights). With technology they set transaction and production costs, and so the incentive structure of an economy. Tribal exchange, the Suq and the caravan trade did not evolve from within; early modern European trade did, through merchant law, bills of exchange, insurance and a state bound not to confiscate. Institutional change is path dependent because the institutional matrix has increasing returns. A narrative essay; the definition is stipulated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-392](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-392.md)); worth reading as the economist's canonical one-paragraph definition of institutions ("the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction") and as a compact statement of the transaction-cost and path-dependence programme. It is an essay, not an argument: the game-theoretic motivation is one paragraph, the history is narrative, and the definition is stipulated, not defended. For what an institution is, read it beside Hindriks & Guala ([LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md)), who take it as the exemplar of the rules account and say what it leaves out. |
| [LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md) v2 | Collective Intentions and Actions | Searle (1990), DOI-10.7551/mitpress/3839.003.0021, in Cohen, Morgan & Pollack (eds.), Intentions in Communication (MIT Press), pp. 401–416; reprinted in Consciousness and Language (2002). The paper in which Searle introduces collective intentionality, intentions of the form "we intend", as a phenomenon of individual minds that is not a sum of individual "I intend" states plus mutual belief. Unread: filed from metadata, and from how Searle's own later paper uses it. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata; no lawful full text was reachable (the MIT Press chapter is paywalled and returned 403, the CUP reprint is paywalled, the Internet Archive copy of the volume is lending-only, and no author or course copy was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the paper that put "collective intentionality" into analytic philosophy and the source Searle's later social ontology ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md)) sends readers to. |
| [LIT-491](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-491.md) v2 | Categories We Live By: The Construction of Sex, Gender, Race, and Other Social Categories | Ásta (2018), OUP. Per its publisher, a theory of social categories built on the question "what is it for a feature of an individual to be socially meaningful?"; its main idea is that "social categories are conferred upon people", and its "conferralist" framework is applied to sex, gender, race, disability and other categories, and to their tendency to oppress. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is not open access, Oxford Academic is paywalled, and the author's site posts replies and related essays but no chapters or drafts), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the book-length statement of conferralism, the main rival to Haslanger's account of social categories ([LIT-480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-480.md)); what it argues beyond the description is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-492](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-492.md) v2 | On Social Facts | Gilbert (1989), Routledge (reissued by Princeton University Press, 1992; DOI-10.1515/9780691214627). The book asks whether social groups are real over and above individuals' thoughts. It analyses everyday concepts of social action, social groups, collective belief and social convention, in dialogue with Weber, Simmel, Durkheim and David Lewis, and proposes that core social phenomena are "plural subject" phenomena. Unread: filed from the publishers' descriptions and the chapter list. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publishers' records and the chapter list; no lawful full text was reachable (the Princeton reissue is sold as an e-book on De Gruyter, and the Internet Archive's copy of the Routledge edition is lending-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is Gilbert's book-length treatment of plural subjects, collective belief and social convention; "Walking Together" ([LIT-477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-477.md)) is the short version. |
| [LIT-493](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-493.md) v2 | The Grammar of Society: The Nature and Dynamics of Social Norms | Bicchieri (2006; print December 2005), DOI-10.1017/CBO9780511616037. Per its publisher, an integrated account, drawing on social psychology, experimental economics and evolutionary game theory, of how social norms such as fairness, cooperation and reciprocity emerge, why and when people follow them, when they attend to the relevant norm, why inefficient norms survive, and how psychological dispositions can lead to fairness norms like ours. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. Cambridge Core is paywalled. The author's own copy of chapter 1 on her University of Pennsylvania pages and the publisher's excerpt at assets.cambridge.org both failed (HTTP 403; connection reset), and the Internet Archive has no copy. It is the standard equilibrium-and-expectations account of social norms; what its definition of a norm says was not seen. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-504](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-504.md) v2 | A Natural History of Human Morality | Tomasello (2016), DOI-10.4159/9780674915855. By the publisher's account, a reconstruction from experiments comparing great apes and children of how early humans became "an ultra-cooperative and, eventually, a moral species". The chapter titles give the steps: an interdependence hypothesis, a second-personal morality of collaborating partners, an "objective" morality of the cultural group, and human morality as "cooperation-plus". Unread: filed from the description and chapter list. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The book is lending-only at the Internet Archive (access-restricted, printdisabled) and paywalled at Harvard University Press and De Gruyter. Its relation to Tomasello's later "The moral psychology of obligation" ([LIT-125](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-125.md), read in [NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md)) is inferred from the chapter titles and that reading, and is labelled as inference. An author's précis exists (Philosophical Psychology, 2018, DOI 10.1080/09515089.2018.1486605) and was not read; it would be the natural first step. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-507](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-507.md) | Moral psychology is relationship regulation: Moral motives for unity, hierarchy, equality, and proportionality | Rai & Fiske (2011), DOI-10.1037/a0021867. Relationship regulation theory: moral judgments are not about features of acts (harm, unfairness, impurity) but about whether acts fit the relationship model in force. Fiske's four relational models each carry a moral motive: Unity (communal sharing), Hierarchy (authority ranking), Equality (equality matching) and Proportionality (market pricing). The motives are universal; cultures differ in where they apply them. So violence, inequality and "impure" acts can be morally required, and purity and ingroup loyalty are one motive. A review, with no new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-405](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-405.md)); worth reading as the relational alternative to both Moral Foundations Theory and morality-as-cooperation, and as the source of the Equality/Proportionality split the MFQ-2 later adopted. It is a theoretical review with no new data. It agrees with morality-as-cooperation that morality exists to sustain cooperative relationships, and differs from it on purity (a Unity motive, the same motive as ingroup loyalty), on harm (violence can be morally required) and on the units (four relational models, not seven game-theoretic problems). |
| [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md) | The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization | Barrett (2017), SCAN 12(1):1–23. The brain runs an internal model of the body in the world for allostasis. Its predictions are "concepts" issued from agranular limbic cortex and refined by prediction error. Interoceptive predictions are felt as affect (valence, arousal). An emotion is an instance of categorizing sensation with an emotion concept, built the same way as any perception. Since instances of an emotion are "created by multiple spatiotemporal patterns" (degeneracy), the categories have no neural essences, and the classical view, basic-emotion and causal appraisal theories included, is rejected. Emotions are "constructions of the world, not reactions to it." | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-434](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-434.md)); worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the theory of constructed emotion and of its link to predictive processing. The brain's core task is allostasis, run through an internal model whose predictions are "concepts". An instance of emotion is what happens when the brain categorizes predicted interoceptive and exteroceptive sensation with an emotion concept. On this account emotion categories have no neural "essences", and causal appraisal theories are "highly doubtful". The paper is a theoretical synthesis: its own data are a few figures, and the rest is cited evidence and explicitly labelled hypotheses. |
| [LIT-567](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-567.md) | A Planning Agent's Self-Governance over Time | Bratman (2018), essay 11 of Planning, Time, and Self-Governance (OUP). A planning agent's self-governance over time is self-governance at each time along a planned activity, plus cross-temporal links of intention that parallel the interlocking intentions of shared agency: in diachronic self-governance one acts "together" with oneself. Standpoints are "diachronicalized" by a conditional, reflexive end of one's own diachronic self-governance. That end can make willpower and resistance to "shuffling" self-governed, while anticipated regret at "plan's end" excludes drinking Kavka's toxin. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-464](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-464.md)), in the author's pre-publication draft of 10 July 2017, not the typeset chapter. Worth reading as the read substitute for Planning, Time, and Self-Governance (2018) and, through its summary of the planning theory, for Intention, Plans, and Practical Reason (1987, [LIT-593](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-593.md)). A planning agent governs herself over time when she is self-governing at each time along a planned activity and her intentions at those times interlock like the intentions of people acting together, so that she acts "together" with herself. Her standpoints are "diachronicalized": they include a conditional, reflexive end of her own diachronic self-governance. That end explains how willpower and resisting "shuffling" between incomparable options can be self-governed, and anticipated regret at plan's end rules out drinking Kavka's toxin. A philosophical model argued by cases; nothing in it is tested. |
| [LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md) | Participatory sense-making: An enactive approach to social cognition | De Jaegher & Di Paolo (2007), Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 6(4):485–507. Coordination between coupled systems is cheap and common. When patterns of coordination and the course of an encounter shape each other, the interaction acquires its own operationally closed, precarious organization. Social interaction is then regulated coupling between autonomous agents that constitutes an autonomous relational organization without destroying the agents' autonomy. Because sense-making is embodied in movement, interactors can coordinate their sense-making, along a spectrum from modulated individual sense-making to jointly created meaning. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md)), from the published version posted on De Jaegher's own site. Worth reading as the founding statement of participatory sense-making. A social interaction is defined as regulated coupling between autonomous agents that itself becomes an autonomous organization in the relational domain, without destroying the agents' autonomy; coordinating sense-making in interaction can generate meanings neither individual had. The argument is conceptual, illustrated by everyday cases and by the perceptual-crossing experiments; nothing is measured in the paper. |
| [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md) | The Normative Constitution of Agency | Korsgaard (2014), in Rational and Social Agency: The Philosophy of Michael Bratman (OUP), pp. 190–214. Two conceptions of agency are set side by side: natural (action is movement caused by the right mental state) and normatively constituted (action is movement backed by a unified agent, whose unity is achieved by following norms). Following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives gives action "the form of self-determined efficacy". Choosing maxims under that form constitutes one's practical identity. Self-consciousness of one's own attitudes sets the task of unification. Unity of agency "is an achievement, not a given", so people can literally act together. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-455](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-455.md)), in the author's posted manuscript, not the typeset chapter. Worth reading as the read substitute for Self-Constitution (2009, [LIT-597](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-597.md)), which it summarises and extends, and as Korsgaard's direct engagement with Bratman. Agency is "normatively constituted": an action is a movement "backed by the agent as a whole", and that unity is achieved by following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives, which give action "the form of self-determined efficacy". The content of the maxims we choose under that form constitutes our "practical identities". So "we make ourselves into agents", and unity of agency, individual or collective, "is an achievement, not a given". Argued, not proved; the account of reason as unification is said to be "lifted" from her other work. |
| [LIT-696](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-696.md) v2 | Towards a Theory of Collective Emotions | von Scheve & Ismer (2013), Emotion Review 5(4):406–413. Collective emotion is synchronous convergence in affective responding towards an event or object. Three literatures (face-to-face contagion and effervescence, culture and shared knowledge, social identification) are recast as bottom-up mechanisms on three levels: social cognition (shared appraisals; collectively intentional appraisals), expressive behaviour (contagion, "facial dialects") and symbolic practice (collective memory, group-based sentiments, norms, cultural sharing). Mutual awareness and group membership amplify convergence and can turn I-mode into We-mode collective emotion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-552](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-552.md)); worth reading as a compact map of how collective emotion has been theorised across sociology, social psychology and philosophy, and as the source of a working definition: collective emotion is synchronous convergence in affective responding across individuals towards one event or object. Shared appraisal structures give the minimal case. Mutual awareness (contagion, sharing) and group membership (identity, collective intention, norms, collective memory, sentiments) amplify it and can turn "I-mode" into "We-mode" collective emotion. A conceptual synthesis with no data, built bottom-up by methodological choice. |
| [LIT-697](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-697.md) v2 | The feeling of being a group: Corporate emotions and collective consciousness | Schmid (2014), in von Scheve & Salmela (eds.), Collective Emotions (OUP), pp. 3–16. Unread. By summaries of its abstract: against the view that groups cannot have emotions because they lack consciousness, it argues that a group with proper intentional attitudes has consciousness, as plural pre-reflective self-awareness, and so meets a precondition for emotion. Groups probably cannot have "fast" emotions but can have "slow" ones such as confidence, happiness or grief. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-04, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The chapter is paywalled at Oxford Academic, Unpaywall finds no open copy, and the University of Vienna's research portal refused the request; the author's preprint is posted only on ResearchGate and academia.edu, which this record does not use. What is said of it comes from summaries of its abstract returned by a search service, labelled unverified. A person could supply the chapter from the OUP volume or ask the author; a reading would move this to Active and should test whether its "corporate emotions" are corporate attitudes in List's sense. |
| [LIT-698](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-698.md) v2 | Collective Guilt | Isaacs (2011), ch. 3 of Moral Responsibility in Collective Contexts (OUP), pp. 71–94. Unread. By a summary of its abstract, it takes collective guilt to be blameworthy collective moral responsibility, a feature of collective agents that does not distribute to members; separates being guilty, believing oneself guilty and feeling guilty, and personal, membership and collective guilt; and, engaging Gilbert, concludes that collectives may be guilty without having guilt feelings. The review in NDPR confirms the non-distribution claim (pp. 81–83). | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-04, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The work the owner means is chapter 3, "Collective Guilt", of Isaacs's Moral Responsibility in Collective Contexts (OUP, 2011); no Monist paper of that title exists. The book is paywalled, and none of Isaacs's shorter papers on collective responsibility (Midwest Studies 2014, New Criminal Law Review 2013) has an open copy. What is said here comes from Matt King's review in Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews (read in full) and from a search-service summary of the chapter abstract (unverified). A person with the book could supply the chapter; a reading would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-700.md) | Three kinds of collective attitudes | List (2014), Erkenntnis 79(S9):1601–1622. Collective attitudes come in three kinds. Aggregate attitudes summarise members' attitudes by a rule or a market, supervene proposition-wise and need not be rational. Common attitudes are held by all members with common awareness, matter for coordination, and inherit consistency from their unanimity. Corporate attitudes belong to a group agent, guide its action, supervene holistically on members' contributions and must be rational. The kinds are almost logically independent, and fears and hopes divide the same way as beliefs and desires. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md)); worth reading as the disambiguation the collective-attitudes literature needs: aggregate attitudes (summaries, supervening proposition by proposition), common attitudes (unanimous and commonly known, supervening on a slightly enriched base) and corporate attitudes (a group agent's, supervening holistically and not straightforwardly reducible). The three are almost logically independent. A review by its own description, with no new theorem; its value for this record is that it names fears and hopes among the attitudes the split applies to, which gives the collective-emotion debate a vocabulary. |
| [LIT-701](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-701.md) v3 | Collective Guilt and Collective Guilt Feelings | Gilbert (2002), The Journal of Ethics 6(2):115–143. Unread. As read sources report it: it distinguishes personal, membership and collective guilt feelings, and defines collective guilt feelings by joint commitment, so that for us collectively to feel guilt over our action is for us to be jointly committed to feel guilt as a body. A plural subject can thus be in a collective emotion, and since emotions are separable from feelings, such emotions need no phenomenology of their own. Reprinted in Gilbert's Joint Commitment (2013), ch. 11. | Unfetched — filed 2026-10-04, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. Springer and the OUP reprint are paywalled, Unpaywall finds no open copy, and the PhilArchive record (GILCGA) and SSRN abstract 1071254 both answered automated requests with a bot challenge or a block, which I did not try to get past. What the record says of it comes from Huebner's read paper, which quotes it with page references, and is labelled second-hand. A person with PhilArchive or library access could supply the text; a reading would move this to Active and should test Huebner's charge that a plural subject's emotion reduces to individual commitments. Free copy: philarchive.org/rec/GILCGA (PhilArchive). |
| [LIT-702](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-702.md) | Genuinely collective emotions | Huebner (2010), European Journal for Philosophy of Science 1(1):89–118. Against the received view that only individuals have emotions, it argues that some groups have the computational complexity and informational integration that emotion requires. Emotions are integrated, action- oriented representations built from subpersonal routines; a distributed system can integrate routines the same way. It answers the objection from consciousness (some individual emotions are non-conscious, so collective ones need not be felt) and from homology (emotion kinds are functional, "like vodka", not "like bourbon"). A navy crew turns out to detect danger without fear; a failing election campaign is offered instead. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-553](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-553.md)); worth reading as the distributed, computational case for collective emotion, and the clearest statement of what it would take. An emotion is an integrated representation with indicative content and imperative force, built from subpersonal routines; a group whose routines are integrated the same way can be in one, without feeling it. The test case fails on the author's own terms (the USS Palau crew detects danger without fear) and the replacement (a 2008 presidential campaign) is offered as intuitively plausible pending anthropology, so the paper establishes a possibility and a research programme, not an instance. |
| [LIT-705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-705.md) | Group Agency and Supervenience | List & Pettit (2006), Southern Journal of Philosophy 44(S1):85–105. A group agent's rationality must supervene on its members' contributions, but not proposition by proposition. Three impossibility results show that robust group rationality (complete, consistent, deductively closed group judgments for every profile of rational member judgments) is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience. Premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures show it is consistent with set-wise supervenience, with group judgments that can be discontinuous with the members' judgments on the same proposition. Emergent agency without any member's conception of the group is set aside as unintelligible. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md)); worth reading as the short, formal core of List and Pettit's group agency: a group can be a robustly rational judge only if its judgment on a proposition is not, in general, a function of its members' judgments on that proposition. Group judgments supervene on members' judgments set-wise, not proposition-wise, so a group agent is individualistically unmysterious and still "not directly continuous" with its members. Read here as the lawful substitute for the unread book [LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md), whose chapter 3 takes up the same supervenience question; the impossibility results are cited from other papers, not proved here. |
| [LIT-718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-718.md) | The Conversable, Responsible Corporation | Pettit (2017), in Orts & Smith (eds), The Moral Responsibility of Firms, OUP, pp. 15–35. Corporations are agents and, through authorised spokespersons, conversable ones that avow attitudes and make promises. Because majority voting on connected judgments can be inconsistent, a conversable corporation must correct its aggregate and so forms a mind of its own. Conversable agents are fit to be held responsible, so corporations are. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-569](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-569.md)): in full, from the manuscript Pettit circulated for a master class at the European University Institute. Worth reading as the short statement of his case that corporations are fit to be held responsible. A corporation is a conversable agent: it speaks for itself through authorised spokespersons and commits itself, rather than reporting its members' attitudes. It must correct for the inconsistency any mechanical aggregation produces, so it has a mind of its own. Conversable agents meet the three conditions of fitness to be held responsible. The chapter stands in for the unread 2007 paper [LIT-742](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-742.md). |
| [LIT-727](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-727.md) | The Corporation as a Moral Person | French (1979), American Philosophical Quarterly 16(3):207–215. A moral person is a non-eliminable subject of accountability, which requires intentional agency. A corporation's Internal Decision (CID) Structure, its organizational chart plus recognition rules in corporate policy, licenses redescribing members' acts as corporate acts done for corporate reasons. So corporations, unlike mobs, can be full-fledged moral persons. That agency suffices for moral personhood is asserted, not argued here. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-568](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-568.md)): in full, from a scanned JSTOR copy in a Brooklyn College instructor's readings folder. Worth reading as the founding statement of the claim that corporations are moral persons. French rests it on the Corporate Internal Decision (CID) Structure: an organizational chart plus recognition rules embedded in corporate policy. It licenses redescribing members' acts as corporate intentional acts. Limits: he asserts, and says he cannot here argue, that intentional agency suffices for moral personhood, and the paper offers no test of corporate intentionality beyond the redescription itself. |
| [LIT-730](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-730.md) | Episteme Symposium on Group Agency: Replies to Gaus, Cariani, Sylvan, and Briggs | List & Pettit (2012), Episteme 9(3):293–309. Replies to a symposium on Group Agency. Ecological rationality is classical rationality relative to an environment; robust group rationality can be relaxed by context, yet proposition-wise aggregation stays very limited. Group attitudes are real and non-redundant: role-based member acceptance does not reduce them. Group agents are fit to be held responsible in their own right but should have restricted rights, on normative individualism. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-582.md)): in full, from the authors' copy on List's LSE pages. Worth reading as the authors' own short commentary on Group Agency ([LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md), unread), which it quotes with page references. It says the premise-based procedure was only ever illustrative, that robust group rationality may be relaxed case by case without rescuing proposition-wise supervenience, that no accessible individualistic recipe makes group attitudes redundant, and that group agents are fit to be held responsible in their own right but should have restricted rights. Limits: replies to commentaries not in the record; the book's claims are seen only as quoted. |
| [LIT-736](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-736.md) | Shaping the Institutional Mind | Tollefsen (2025), Philosophies 10(5):112. Advocates and critics of group minds share the "standard view" that ascribing attitudes tracks pre-existing causes. On McGeer's regulative view, ascription shapes its target. Ascribing knowledge to institutions, as in the collective knowledge doctrine, and issuing institutional narratives shape institutions to be more agent-like. The view stays agnostic about whether institutions really have minds. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-570](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-570.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY 4.0). Worth reading for a different answer to why we ascribe beliefs and knowledge to institutions: not because the ascriptions describe pre-existing states, but because, on the regulative view of folk psychology, they shape institutions to be more agent-like. Its main case is the collective knowledge doctrine in corporate criminal law, after which banks built systems to detect reporting violations. Limits: the regulative view is assumed, not argued; the causal story about banks is asserted without evidence; and the paper is agnostic about whether institutions have minds. It does not stand in for her book Groups as Agents ([LIT-483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-483.md)), which stays unread. |
| [LIT-742](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-742.md) v2 | Responsibility Incorporated | Pettit (2007), Ethics 117:171–201. Incorporated groups face significant choices, can recognise the relative value of their options, and can choose in sensitivity to those values, so they meet the conditions for being fit to be held responsible. Unread: the argument is read in his 2017 chapter [LIT-718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-718.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (SSRN's download is blocked to this client, and the journal is closed). | [LIT-848](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-848.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Farrell, Gopnik, Shalizi & Evans (2025), Science 387(6739):1153–1156, Policy Forum. | [LIT-897](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-897.md) v2 | AI as Agency without Intelligence: On Artificial Intelligence as a New Form of Artificial Agency and the Multiple Realisability of Agency Thesis | Floridi (2025), DOI-10.1007/s13347-025-00858-9. An Editor Letter that "grew so long". AI is better understood by widening agency to forms without cognition, intelligence or mental states than by widening intelligence to machines. Agency comes in kinds (natural, biological, animal social, artefactual, human individual and social, artificial, social artificial). All of them share interactivity, and the richer ones add graded autonomy and adaptability. AI is computational, data-adaptive agency serving goals set by humans, with no intelligence. The thesis is assumed, and the paper characterises the kind rather than arguing for it. The criteria do not separate AI from other artefacts, and no level of abstraction is stated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-702](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-702.md)); worth reading for the fullest statement of Floridi's position that AI is "agency without intelligence": the Multiple Realisability of Agency thesis set against the Artificial Realisability of Intelligence, Floridi & Sanders' three criteria restated as graded, and a taxonomy that places AI as "a computational, goal-driven form of agency defined by human purposes" with Agentic AI as its collective form. Read it as a taxonomy, not an argument. The case for MRA over ARI is announced and not made, since the paper assumes AI is an agent and asks what kind. AI's lack of intelligence is asserted. | [LIT-898](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-898.md) v2 | On the Morality of Artificial Agents | Floridi & Sanders (2004), DOI-10.1023/B:MIND.0000035461.63578.9d. Whether something is an agent is fixed only relative to a level of abstraction (LoA), a chosen set of observables. At a suitable LoA a system is an agent if it is interactive, autonomous (changes state without stimulus) and adaptable (its interactions change its transition rules); humans, learning software and organisations all qualify. An agent is a moral agent if it can cause moral good or evil. Such an agent is accountable for what it causes, but responsibility (praise and blame) needs intentional states as well, so artificial agents can be moral agents that are accountable and not responsible, and are censured by modification, disconnection or deletion. The argument is by cases and by rebutting four objections. The paper's own MENACE example shows agenthood appearing and vanishing as the LoA changes. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-701](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-701.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of Floridi's line on artificial agency: agenthood as interactivity, autonomy and adaptability at a stated level of abstraction, and moral agency as the capacity to cause moral good or evil, with accountability split from responsibility. Read §2.5, §2.6.2 (MENACE) and §3.2 for the position. It argues by cases and by rebutting four objections; nothing in it is derived, the permissiveness of its criteria is answered by assertion (p. 26), and the distributed morality it says the approach is for is promised, not worked out. |
| [LIT-901](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-901.md) v2 | Distributed Morality in an Information Society | Floridi (2013), DOI-10.1007/s11948-012-9413-4. Distributed morality is the case where morally loaded actions of a human, artificial or hybrid multiagent system result from interactions among its members that are each morally neutral or negligible, modelled on distributed knowledge (A knows P∨Q, B knows ¬P, only the "supra-agent" AB knows Q). Two moral thresholds make environments fault-tolerant to small evils and inert to small goods, so managing distributed morality means aggregating possible goods and fragmenting possible evils. ICTs make it common. "Infraethics" is the first-order framework of moral enablers (trust, privacy, transparency …) that is not good in itself. The analogy is looser than it looks: every example sums like contributions past a threshold whose value is left open. Responsibility for distributed morality is not addressed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-698.md)); worth reading as the line's only worked statement of distributed morality (morally loaded actions of a multiagent system arising from interactions each below a moral threshold) and as the source of "infraethics", the first-order framework of moral enablers that is not morally good in itself. Read pp. 729–734 for the threshold model and pp. 738–740 for infraethics. It argues by a model and four examples and proves nothing. Its analogy with distributed knowledge is not exact: every example sums like contributions past a threshold whose value is left unspecified. No criterion of agency is applied to its "supra-agents", and responsibility for distributed morality, which Floridi & Sanders 2004 promised, is still not given. |

| [LIT-1043](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1043.md) | Intention and Convention in Speech Acts | Strawson (1964), The Philosophical Review 73(4):439–460. Against Austin, many illocutions are not conventional: a warning to a skater, an entreaty, an objection. What all illocutions share is an overt intention meant to be understood. | Active — read 2026-10-13 ([NOTE-736](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-736.md)) in full; worth reading as the step from Grice's speaker meaning to illocutionary force: an illocution not essentially conventional is an act of communication whose force is a wholly overt, audience-directed intention, while acts like a verdict or an umpire's call exist only within rule-governed procedures. Read it knowing that its own scheme strains on orders and fails on institutional acts, and that it individuates request from entreaty by a recognised attitude of the speaker. The memory is a property of the functional system, "not made primarily of pilot memory", though pilot memory is involved. Stylized and unmeasured, for an anticipated, invariant task. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the author's posted copy, a scan of the published article (Cognitive Science 19(3), pp. 265–288) at pages.ucsd.edu/~ehutchins/documents/CockpitSpeeds.pdf. For [QUESTION-101](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-101.md) and [CLAIM-296](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-296.md) it shows, by task analysis and not by measurement, a change of arrangement alone changing what the system can do; the retrieval cue (displayed gross weight, the needle nearing a bug) supplied by the environment; and the work of retrieval moved to a quiet phase 25 to 30 minutes ahead of use, which the record's deadline does not yet represent. Group identification, as the shared-agency literature uses it, conflates adopting the group's perspective (team reasoning) with self-transformation (understanding oneself as a member). The two dissociate: the discursive dilemma shows perspective without identification, and toddlers' joint action shows identification before perspective-taking appears. Self-transformation is a Pushmi-Pullyu representation, describing and motivating at once ("you are a member of us; act as such"), and is not under direct rational control. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1266](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1266.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript in University College Cork's repository (CORA); worth reading as the distinction between adopting a group's perspective and the self-transformation of identifying as a member, the second cast as a Pushmi-Pullyu representation that motivates directly, and for its team reasoner versus team benefactor, which sharpens the owner's thesis ([CLAIM-491](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-491.md)). Conceptual. |
| [LIT-1698](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1698.md) | Team Reasoning and Intentional Cooperation for Mutual Benefit | Sugden (2015). Social preferences cannot represent trust: on Rabin-style intention-based preferences, the common-knowledge practice of trust in the Trust Game is not an equilibrium. Team reasoning can, but not Bacharach's version, which maximizes a team utility, trades members' interests off against each other and needs no assurance that others reason as a team. Sugden's Schema of Cooperative Team Reasoning aims at each member's benefit over a maximin benchmark, follows existing practices and binds only given reciprocal reason to believe the others endorse it. So a market exchange that serves each party's interest can still be intended as mutual benefit, neither self-interest nor sacrifice. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1288](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1288.md)) from the published version, open under CC BY-NC-ND at the Journal of Social Ontology; worth reading as Sugden's own later statement of team reasoning, read in place of his 2003 paper ([LIT-1782](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1782.md), Unavailable), and for its claim that team reasoning cannot be reduced to self-interest or to social preferences by redefining payoffs, which bears on the owner's thesis ([CLAIM-491](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-491.md)). |
| [LIT-1721](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1721.md) | Being one of us: we-identities and self-categorization theory | León (2023). A we-identity is one a subject has as a group member, is at times aware of, endorses, and cares about. Self-categorization theory explains we-identities by depersonalization, and phenomenologists (Zahavi, Salice) have adopted it as an account of the "we" in general. But the we-identities of close relationships arise by mutual individualization: partners grasp each other as non-substitutable and complementary. León proposes a socially extended account, drawing on Husserl and integrationist extended-mind criteria. | Active — read in full 2026-10-28 ([NOTE-1309](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1309.md)) from the open-access published article; worth reading as a philosopher's limit on self-categorization theory: the we-identities of close relationships (long friendships, romantic partnerships) rest on mutual individualization and non-substitutability, the opposite of depersonalization, so the theory cannot be the general account of the "we" that phenomenologists have taken it to be. It proposes a socially extended account of such identities. An argument from cases and from relationship research, with no data of its own. Source of [THEORY-1115](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1115.md). |
| [LIT-1723](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1723.md) | Rediscovering the Social Group: A Self-Categorization Theory | Turner, Hogg, Oakes, Reicher and Wetherell (1987), Blackwell. The founding statement of self-categorization theory: personal and social identity are levels of self-categorization, a category becomes salient by meta-contrast and fit, and group behaviour follows from depersonalization, self-perception as an interchangeable exemplar of the ingroup prototype, rather than from attraction or interdependence among members. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-28; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. (LIT-1790). |
| [LIT-1744](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1744.md) | A Social Identity Model of Deindividuation Phenomena | Reicher, Spears & Postmes (1995). The SIDE model: anonymity in a group does not remove identity, it shifts it from the personal to the social level, so people become more responsive to the salient group norm, prosocial or antisocial; strategic effects depend on visibility to the in-group and out-group. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. | [LIT-1758](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1758.md) | Second-Person Engagement, Self-Alienation, and Group-Identification | Zahavi (2016/2019) reconstructs and defends Husserl's empathy-based account of the "we" against Heidegger and Hans Bernhard Schmid. Truly social acts need a second-person relation: an I–Thou relation of reciprocal, communicative address, in which I am aware of the other and of myself as addressed by them. Taking over the other's perspective on oneself, a self-apprehension Husserl calls "self-alienation", lets the difference between self and other stay present but be "somewhat downplayed", and that is a formal condition of coming to see oneself as "one of us". A we is "not an enlarged I": it preserves plurality and is not fusion. Zahavi likens the condition to self-categorization theory's self-stereotyping, while noting that Husserl attends far more to the interpersonal encounter beneath it. Against Schmid he argues that the sense of "us" can be analysed, that not every social relation is a we, and that children's self-awareness precedes their in-group bias. He concedes that an account built on the dyadic face-to-face "we" does not cover anonymous, institutional "we"s. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1289](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1289.md)) from the peer-reviewed accepted manuscript in the University of Copenhagen's repository (curis.ku.dk); worth reading as the phenomenologist's case that coming to see oneself as one of us is a change in how one apprehends oneself, through another's eyes, and that the resulting "we" is a plurality, not an enlarged I. |
| [LIT-1765](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1765.md) | Reconceptualizing Individuals, Categories, and the Social Group: Self-Categorization Theory 2.0 | Skorich (2025, v2 2026), preprint. Five critiques of self-categorization theory as stated in Turner et al. 1987: categorization into equivalence classes is neither sufficient nor necessary for perceiving a group as an entity; "self-categorization" is underspecified and should mean categorization of intentional agents; the person level is underexamined; meta-contrast is computationally intractable as a basis for entity formation and rests on prototype semantics; and comparative relations are overemphasized. Proposes SCT2.0 (self-conceptualization theory): groups are perceived from cues to collective intentionality, and represented as atomic concepts with object files in a language of thought. | Active — read in full 2026-10-28 ([NOTE-1295](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1295.md)) from the PsyArXiv preprint, v2; worth reading as a sympathetic insider's critique of self-categorization theory that quotes the 1987 book's chapter 3 assumptions and hypotheses verbatim with page numbers, so it stands in for the unread book's core statement. It argues that categorization yields interchangeability, not a group entity; that meta-contrast is computationally intractable as a basis for entity formation; and that groups are perceived from cues to collective intentionality. Unreviewed; its key experiments are under review. Source of [THEORY-1112](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1112.md). |
